After this page you can
  • say, for each claim of Part III of the paper, what supports it and how strong we think it is (solid, suggestive, speculative), and defend that verdict in one sentence;
  • repair the definition of the hypothesis (a union over active sets, not a sum over all tiles) and prove that a bounded linear code is the special case with segment tiles; say what remains to separate the two hypotheses (a box or a simplex inside a tile);

0. Before you start#

Parts I and II of the paper are measurements and stand. Part III proposes a hypothesis and offers evidence for it; this page, which follows the project report (sections 4 and 5), shows that the evidence does not separate the hypothesis from simpler pictures, and that one exact consequence of it fails after the last layer normalisation. It does not show that the hypothesis is false.

How to read this page#

The page is the project's own reading. Boxes marked In the paper quote or paraphrase the paper, with a page reference; they are kept short because pages 3 to 5 develop them. Everything else, in particular every box marked “Our reading” and every experiment, is ours: we say “we” for the arguments of the report. Boxes marked “Checked on DINOv2” and the tables in section 8 point to the results files. A proof is in a fold; read the idea box first.

Three statuses are used for a claim: solid (proved, or measured directly), suggestive (consistent with the data, not separated from rivals) and speculative (not tested, or contradicted by our checks). own marks a result of the project.

Pitfall — “we showed the paper is wrong”

The report does not say that. It says three things: the definition needs a repair; the arguments given do not discriminate between the hypothesis and simpler models; one exact consequence (a Minkowski sum for normalised tokens) is excluded. The authors call their hypothesis “a working hypothesis” and their evidence “compatible, not proof”; the report agrees with that wording and asks what would count as evidence.

The argument of the report in six steps#

  1. Repair and nest. The definition as written clashes with itself (a full sum is convex; the text describes a union). Repaired, it contains bounded linear codes as the case where every tile is a segment. The two hypotheses differ by one thing: inside a group of features, a box or a simplex (section 2).
  2. Delimit the attention argument. “Attention outputs convex combinations” is true for any weights and any input; the polytopes are rebuilt for every image; the condition for filling a polytope fails (rank 64 against 261); a token is mostly not an attention update (section 3).
  3. Layer normalisation. After the last normalisation all tokens lie on an ellipsoid, which contains no segment: no non-trivial Minkowski sum describes them exactly (section 4).
  4. Null models for the three signatures. Chords leave a sample of a Gaussian too; per-image k-means matches the reported error and archetypal analysis sits where a Gaussian puts it; blocks follow image classes, the mark of a union, not of a sum (section 5).
  5. Identifiability. The proof has a gap, repaired; the true statement is about supports and holds for linear codes too; what identifies a dictionary is sparsity and the law of the codes (section 6).
  6. A tile one can observe. The position code is additive in rows and columns to 97%: a box, the linear special case (section 7).

What you need#

  • From page 2: convex hull, simplex, Minkowski sum, zonotopes, support functions, decomposability, stable rank, archetypal analysis and its sandwich, softmax.
  • From page 5: the definition, the attention results, the three pieces of evidence and the identifiability result. The notation is the one of page 5; X is a set of activations here.

1. The verdict, claim by claim#

Parts I and II are measurements and are not contested. In Part III, the mathematics is correct where it is a theorem, the arguments for the hypothesis do not separate it from simpler pictures, and one consequence fails exactly after the last normalisation.

The table lists the claims of Part III of the paper (page 5), what supports each, our status for it, and the section of this page that explains why.

What the report does not contest#

Parts I and II of the paper: which atoms each task uses, the Elsewhere and border concepts, the token-type footprints, the geometry of the dictionary (dense positional atoms, anisotropy, antipodal pairs, the smooth token clouds). They are measurements of a trained dictionary on a trained model, with figures one can inspect; the report only uses them. It also does not contest the mathematics of Lemma 1 and Proposition 1, and it agrees that the hypothesis is a legitimate and fruitful one, since it asks whether features compete inside groups, a question the linear hypothesis cannot even state.

What the report contests#

Four things. (1) The definition of the hypothesis, which needs a repair, and its relation to the linear hypothesis, which it contains. (2) The inference from “attention outputs convex combinations” to “the representation is a Minkowski sum of polytopes fixed across images”. (3) The three empirical signatures, which data without archetypes also produce. (4) The identifiability consequence, whose proof has a gap and whose repaired statement is not specific to the hypothesis. Each is a statement about the argument; none is a proof that tokens are not sums of convex combinations of something.

Reflex

When you see “evidence for the hypothesis” → ask which simpler picture produces the same figure, and whether the authors ran it. Most of this page is that question, asked three times.

2. Box or simplex: the two hypotheses are nested#

Repaired, the Minkowski hypothesis describes a union of polytopes over active sets. A bounded linear code is the case where every tile is a segment. What is left to tell the two apart is the constraint that couples the codes inside a group: a box (free) or a simplex (a shared unit budget).

The definition needs one repair#

In the paper Def. 2 · p. 18, App. J · p. 46

Archetypes A=(a1​,…,ac​) are partitioned into tiles T1​,…,Tm​ with polytopes Pi​=conv(ATi​​). The set of activations satisfies (i) X=P1​⊕⋯⊕Pm​, and (ii) every activation is block-convex: x=∑i∈S​zi​ATi​​ with each zi​ in a simplex and ∣S∣≪m. The text adds “a union over attention patterns when different tiles are selected across inputs”. Detail on page 5.

The problem. A Minkowski sum of convex sets is convex, and a point of P1​⊕⋯⊕Pm​ receives one contribution from every tile. Item (ii) lets only a few tiles contribute. The two items agree only if an inactive tile contributes a fixed point (for instance {0}). The set the text really describes, with its “union”, is

X=S∈S⋃​ i∈S⨁​Pi​,

a union of polytopes indexed by the admissible active sets S. This is the exact counterpart of sparse coding, whose activations fill a union of low-dimensional cones.

Our reading — why this matters for the evidence

Under the full sum, X is convex, so “a straight line between two tokens leaves the data” cannot be evidence for (i): a convex set contains the whole chord. Under the union it can, but only if the two tokens use different active sets. The repair makes the hypothesis precise enough to be tested; it is not an objection to it.

A bounded linear code is a Minkowski code with segment tiles#

Proposition — nested hypotheses own

(a) Let x=∑j∈S​zj​dj​ with ∣S∣≤k and 0≤zj​≤M. Then x satisfies the block-convex form (ii) with the same active set and the two-point tiles Tj​={0,Mdj​}. With signed codes ∣zj​∣≤M, use Tj​={−Mdj​,Mdj​}.

(b) Conversely, a code satisfying (ii) is a non-negative linear code over the dictionary of archetypes, with at most ∑i∈S​∣Ti​∣ non-zero entries, subject to the ∣S∣ equalities ∑j∈Ti​​zj​=1.

Idea

A number in [0,M] is a convex combination of its two ends 0 and M. So a bounded coefficient times a direction is a point of the segment from the origin to Mdj​, and the segment is a tile with two archetypes. Every other statement follows from this one line.

Proof, step by step
  1. Take j∈S and λj​=zj​/M∈[0,1].because 0≤zj​≤M
  2. zj​dj​=(1−λj​)0+λj​(Mdj​).multiply out: λj​Mdj​=zj​dj​
  3. This is a convex combination of the two archetypes of Tj​={0,Mdj​}, with code (1−λj​,λj​) in the simplex Δ2.the weights are non-negative and sum to 1
  4. Sum over j∈S: x=∑j∈S​((1−λj​)0+λj​Mdj​), one point per active tile. This is (ii).definition of block-convex coding
  5. Signed case: for ∣zj​∣≤M put λj​=(zj​+M)/(2M)∈[0,1]. Then (1−λj​)(−Mdj​)+λj​(Mdj​)=(2λj​−1)Mdj​=zj​dj​.2λj​−1=zj​/M
  6. (b): a block-convex code writes x=∑i∈S​∑j∈Ti​​zj​aj​ with zj​≥0 and ∑j∈Ti​​zj​=1 for each i∈S. Read it as x=zA with z≥0 supported on ⋃i∈S​Ti​.it is a rewriting of (ii): a non-negative linear code on the archetypes with ∣S∣ sum-to-one constraints
Worked example with numbers

In the plane take d1​=(1,0), d2​=(0.6,0.8) (unit vectors), M=2 and z=(1.5,0.5). The linear code gives x=1.5(1,0)+0.5(0.6,0.8)=(1.8,0.4). In the tile form: λ=(0.75,0.25); tile 1 is {0,(2,0)} and contributes 0.75(2,0)=(1.5,0); tile 2 is {0,(1.2,1.6)} and contributes 0.25(1.2,1.6)=(0.3,0.4); the sum is (1.8,0.4). With a signed code, z1​=−0.5 gives λ1​=(−0.5+2)/4=0.375 on the tile {−2d1​,2d1​}: 0.625(−2,0)+0.375(2,0)=(−0.5,0).

Since activations are bounded, the proposition says that every representation satisfying the linear hypothesis satisfies the Minkowski one, with segments as tiles: its set of activations is a union of zonotopes. Conversely a tile with two archetypes {a,b} contributes a+λ(b−a): a bounded linear feature along b−a with an offset. The two hypotheses therefore part ways only at tiles with three archetypes or more.

What is left: the budget inside a tile#

For a tile {a,b,c} the points are a+λb​(b−a)+λc​(c−a). Under the Minkowski hypothesis the coordinates (λb​,λc​) satisfy λb​,λc​≥0 and λb​+λc​≤1: a triangle. Under the linear hypothesis, where the two features are free to be large together, they fill the square [0,1]2. Inside a tile, features share a unit budget; across tiles they do not. A tile is an irreducible multi-dimensional feature in the sense of Engels et al., and the hypothesis is the linear one plus a statement of mutual exclusion inside groups of atoms: a categorical variable relaxed to its simplex.

Worked example with numbers — the budget decides

Tile a=(0,0), b=(2,0), c=(0,2). The point with λ=(0.5,0.25) is (1,0.5), budget 0.75≤1: both hypotheses allow it. The point with λ=(0.75,0.75) is (1.5,1.5), budget 1.5>1: only the box allows it. The set of activations is the triangle of area 2 for the simplex and the square [0,2]2 of area 4 for the box. If the codes were uniform on the box, half of them would violate the budget.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: in “triangle” mode no sample has z1​+z2​>1 and the activations fill a triangle of half the area of the parallelogram; in “box” mode the corner (1,1) is reached. Lower the concentration α below 1: the points go to the corners of the feasible set (near the archetypes), which is what “activations concentrate near archetypes” means. Change the angle between g1​,g2​: the parallelogram shears, the question “box or triangle?” does not depend on it. This is the quantity the hypothesis adds, and it concerns the codes, not the set.

The hexagon: one support, two hypotheses#

The budget is a property of the codes, not of the set they generate. Let g1​,g2​,g3​ be unit vectors at 0∘,60∘,120∘, Sk​=[−gk​/2,gk​/2], and T an equilateral triangle of unit side centred at the origin. The regular hexagon H of unit circumradius satisfies

H=S1​⊕S2​⊕S3​=T⊕(−T).

The first expression is a linear code with three bounded features in superposition in the plane; the second is a block-convex code with two ternary tiles. We checked it numerically (t4_hexagon.json): both sums have six vertices, and their support functions agree with the hexagon's on 720 directions to 6×10−16. In direction 0∘, for example, the three segments give 21​(1+21​+21​)=1 and the two triangles give hT​+h−T​=21​+21​=1.

How to read this figure
  • Panels (a)–(b). The same regular hexagon written as a Minkowski sum in two ways: three segments at 0∘,60∘,120∘ (a linear code with three bounded features), and a triangle plus its reflection (a code with two three-way tiles).
  • Panels (c)–(d). Two clouds of 4,000 points with the same hexagonal support. (c) sparse independent linear codes (tk​=0 with probability 0.7, else uniform in [−21​,21​]): mass near the centre and along the three lines spanned by the generators. (d) block-convex codes, Dirichlet(0.3) on T and on −T: mass near the nine sums of vertices, the diagonals and the boundary.
  • What to look at. The support is identical; the clouds are told apart at a glance. Numerically, the largest excess of each cloud over the hexagon's support function is ≤0 (inside), and the covariance of (c) is about 0.037I while that of (d) is about 0.17I.
  • Conclusion. A test of the Minkowski hypothesis against the linear one must bear on the joint statistics of the codes; a test that only asks where activations lie cannot succeed.
  • What it does not show. It is a toy in the plane; it does not say which law real codes follow.
Checked — t4_hexagon (a, b)

Vertex and support-function errors of both decompositions on 720 directions: below 6×10−16. Both clouds lie in the hexagon (maximal excess over its support function: −0.033 and −1.2×10−4). See section 8.

3. What the attention argument shows#

“A head outputs a convex combination of its values, and heads add up” is a correct statement about softmax. It does not say that the representation is a Minkowski sum of fixed polytopes, for four reasons, each with a measured number.

In the paper Lemma 1, Prop. 1 · p. 19, App. J · p. 47–48

A head with attention weights α∈Δt and values v1​,…,vt​ outputs ∑j​αj​vj​∈conv{vj​}; with H heads and output projections WO(h)​, the layer's output lies in ⨁h=1H​WO(h)​conv{vh,j​}j​, because linear maps send hulls to hulls. The inclusion is an equality if the logits of each head can reach every vector of Rt up to a constant. Full statements and proofs: page 5.

We take this statement as correct (it is: softmax weights are positive and sum to one). The report asks what it implies for the tokens that the dictionary is trained on. Four observations delimit it. The measurements are on 100 Imagenette images with the trained model and its random-weights twin; the script is r4_attention_anatomy.py, the results r4_attention_anatomy.json (section 8).

1. The polytopes are rebuilt for every image#

The values of head h are vh,j​=WV(h)​LN(xj​), where x1​,…,xt​ are the tokens of the current image at the previous layer. The polytope conv{vh,j​}j​ is a function of the image. The statement says that the update of a token is a mixture of the other tokens of its image, seen through H linear maps. It holds verbatim for a network with random weights and for an input of pure noise: it cannot by itself explain anything that DINOv2 has learned. The hypothesis is a stronger claim, that of a fixed dictionary of archetypes shared by all images; it would require the values of all images to concentrate near a common finite set, which the statement does not address.

2. Equality is out of reach#

The logits of a head are Kq, where the rows of K∈Rt×dk​ are the keys and q∈Rdk​ the query. They span a space of dimension at most dk​=64 (65 with the softmax shift), while equality asks for rankK+1≥t=261. In addition the query of a token is tied to that token, so an image realises exactly t points of each polytope.

64numerical rank of the 261×64 key matrix, every head and image of the last block
261rank + 1 needed for equality
33–78equivalent number of tokens attended to (eentropy), last block, depending on the head
10–49%attention mass on the five special tokens, last block, depending on the head

Attention is also far from the sharp regime in which outputs sit on vertices (low temperature): a patch token attends on average to the equivalent of 33 to 78 tokens out of 261, and puts 10% to 49% of its mass, depending on the head, on the 5 special tokens (class and registers), which hold 5 of 261 tokens, about 2%.

What was measured, and what it does and does not show
  • Rank. Numerical rank of the key matrix of each head of the last block (singular values above smax​⋅261⋅εfloat32​), with and without a column of ones: 64 and 65 in every case. It shows that the condition of Lemma 1 fails by a factor 4; it does not show that the outputs are far from the polytope's interior, only that they cannot fill it.
  • Spread. For each head and token, the entropy of its attention row, exponentiated (“effective number of tokens”), averaged over images and patch tokens. 33 to 78 in the last block; 1.5 to 210 over all 144 heads. It shows that the outputs are averages over many values, not vertices.
  • Special-token mass. Share of the row on cls and the four registers: 10% to 49% in the last block. It shows that a large part of every output is the same few tokens; it does not show these tokens carry no information.

3. An update is not a token#

The representation that is analysed is the residual stream, x(L)=x(0)+∑ℓ​a(ℓ)+∑ℓ​m(ℓ), where a(ℓ) are attention updates and m(ℓ) outputs of MLPs, to which the attention statement does not apply. We verified the identity numerically (largest absolute error 3×10−5 on entries of size up to 176) and projected each term on the final token.

Share of the final tokenembeddingattention (∑ℓ​a(ℓ))MLP (∑ℓ​m(ℓ))
tokens as they are0.0010.650.35
after removing the mean token of each image0.00020.460.54

The share of a term is ⟨term,x(L)⟩/∥x(L)∥2, pooled over tokens; the three shares sum to 1 exactly. Removing the mean token of each image is what isolates the geometry within an image, which is what the signatures study. More than half of that structure is therefore produced by maps that are not convex combinations. The last block alone carries 82% of the token (70% after centring).

What this does and does not show

It shows that “attention builds the geometry” is not the whole story for DINOv2-B: the MLPs contribute a larger share of the within-image variation than attention does. It does not show that MLPs destroy convex structure, and the projection is a linear accounting, not a causal one: the share of a term is not what would be lost by removing it.

4. All heads are active, always#

With tiles equal to heads, every tile is active for every token: ∣S∣=H, so there is no block sparsity (the hypothesis asks ∣S∣≪m). Across the 144 heads of the model, the participation ratio of the per-head update norms of a token is between 5 and 11 heads out of 12 in each block (vi_heads_per_token), and a large share of heads exceeds 10% of the largest update. The sparsity of the hypothesis would have to come from elsewhere.

Our reading — what survives

The attention statement gives a natural candidate for the “codes” of a decomposition: the weights α. That makes the per-head analysis recommended by the paper a sensible place to look for tiles, with two caveats from this section: all heads are active, and the polytopes move with the image.

A colleague says: “attention outputs convex combinations, so the last layer is a Minkowski sum.” Give two independent objections.

Answer

(1) The polytopes are made of the current image's own tokens, so they change with every image and the statement holds for random weights; it does not give a fixed dictionary. (2) Tokens are residual sums of attention and MLP updates and then normalised; the within-image structure is 54% MLP, and the final LayerNorm is not affine. (Also: rank 64 against 261, so the polytope cannot be filled.)

4. No segment after layer normalisation#

The last layer normalisation puts every token on an ellipsoid. An ellipsoid contains no segment, so no non-trivial Minkowski sum of polytopes can be contained in it: the hypothesis, as a statement about the set of normalised tokens, can only be a local approximation.

In the paper footnote 5, App. G.3

The authors describe the activations as lying on an “ellipsoidal geometry” (footnote 5). In App. G.3 they argue that many normalisations become affine once the mean and variance are held fixed. That is true for batch normalisation; LayerNorm uses the statistics of each token, computed at inference, so it is not affine (see errata).

What LayerNorm does to a vector#

The standard features of DINOv2 are read after a final normalisation

LN(x)=γ⊙σ(x)x−μ(x)1​+β,
where μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the coordinates of x, and γ,β are learned. Three steps: centre (subtract the mean coordinate), scale (divide by the standard deviation), then a fixed per-coordinate stretch and shift. The first two steps depend on x through μ and σ, so the map is not affine.

Worked example in dimension 3

Take x=(1,2,6). Then μ=3, deviations (−2,−1,3), variance (4+1+9)/3=14/3, σ=2.160, and u=(−0.926,−0.463,1.389). Check: ∑uk​=0 and ∥u∥2=0.857+0.214+1.929=3=d. The vector 2x=(2,4,12) gives the same u: scale is forgotten. With γ=(1,2,0.5) and β=(0.1,0,−0.1) the output is y=(−0.826,−0.926,0.594).

Whatever x is, u lies in the plane 1⊥ on the circle of radius 3​. Another point of that circle: u′=(1.414,−0.707,−0.707) (from x′=(4,1,1)). Their midpoint is (0.244,−0.585,0.341), of norm 0.720, not 3​=1.732: the midpoint is 1.012 inside the circle. No input x produces it.

The statement and its proof#

Proposition — no segment after layer normalisation own

Assume γk​=0 for all k and neglect the stabilising constant in σ. Then the range of LN is contained in an ellipsoid E of dimension d−2, and:

(a) for two distinct outputs y=y′, no point (1−s)y+sy′ with 0<s<1 belongs to E;

(b) if a set X⊆E is a Minkowski sum P1​⊕⋯⊕Pm​, then every Pi​ is a single point.

Idea

Before the stretch by γ, the points lie on a round sphere, and the midpoint of two distinct points of a sphere is strictly inside it. An invertible affine map keeps “strictly inside” and “on the surface”. A sum that contained a non-trivial summand would contain a whole segment of the surface, which is impossible.

Full proof
  1. Let u=(x−μ(x)1)/σ(x). Then 1⊤u=0 and ∥u∥2=d.the mean of u is 0 and its variance (mean of squares) is 1, so ∑uk2​=d
  2. So u lies on the sphere S={u∈1⊥:∥u∥=d​}, of dimension d−2.a sphere in a hyperplane of dimension d−1
  3. The map Φ(u)=γ⊙u+β is affine and injective.γk​=0: a diagonal matrix with non-zero entries is invertible
  4. The range of LN is contained in E=Φ(S), an ellipsoid.the image of a sphere by an invertible affine map
  5. (a) Take u=u′ in S and s∈(0,1). Then ∥(1−s)u+su′∥2=d−2s(1−s)(d−u⊤u′)<d.expand; u⊤u′<d by Cauchy–Schwarz with equality only if u=u′ (same norm)
  6. So the open segment between u and u′ misses S. Its image by Φ is the open segment between y and y′, and it misses Φ(S).Φ is affine (segments to segments) and injective (a point of E has one preimage in S)
  7. (b) Suppose some Pi​ contains p=p′. Choose qj​∈Pj​ for j=i.the polytopes are non-empty
  8. Then ∑j=i​qj​+[p,p′]⊆X⊆E is a non-degenerate segment inside E.definition of the Minkowski sum
  9. This contradicts (a).(a) says no non-degenerate segment lies in E: its endpoints are two points of E and its interior is not
Remark — the two assumptions are harmless here

γk​=0. Measured on DINOv2-B: 0.19≤∣γk​∣≤14.9 (median 0.96), none below 0.05, none negative. If some γk​ were zero, Φ would project the sphere and its image could be a solid body, which does contain segments: this is why the assumption is needed, and why we measured it. The stabilising constant. The code adds ε=10−6 to the variance; it makes ∥u∥2=dvar/(var+ε), slightly below d (here by about 4×10−7 relative), so tokens sit on a sphere of a radius that varies by 4×10−7: the proof is unchanged.

Checked on DINOv2 — r1_layernorm_ellipsoid

On all 256,000 tokens of 1,000 images, u=(y−β)/γ has a mean coordinate of at most 3.7×10−8 in absolute value, ∣var−1∣≤4.3×10−7 and ∥u∥/d​ between 0.9999998 and 1.0000002: the constraint holds to a relative precision of 10−7. The model's own normalisation, recomputed from the pre-norm tokens, agrees to 2×10−6. For comparison the pre-norm tokens have norms between 80 and 236 (coefficient of variation 0.13), the post-norm ones 19 to 31 (0.056): the normalisation is what makes them lie on a surface.

The depth of a chord#

How far is the midpoint of a chord from the surface? Take two points of S subtending an angle θ at the centre (at the origin of 1⊥). The midpoint is at distance d​cos(θ/2) from the centre, because it lies on the bisector at d​ times the cosine of half the angle. Its depth below the sphere is therefore

(1−cos2θ​)d​,which is tan4θ​ times the half-chord d​sin2θ​.
Worked example

θ=60∘: depth =(1−cos30∘)d​=0.134d​, and the ratio to the half-chord is tan15∘=0.268. For θ=90∘ it is 0.293d​, ratio tan22.5∘=0.414; for θ=180∘ (opposite points) the midpoint is the centre: depth d​, ratio 1.

On the real ellipsoid the shortest way to the surface is not along the ray from the centre. We measured it exactly (the true Euclidean distance to the ellipsoid, by the secular equation) on 2,000 pairs of tokens of the same image and 2,000 of different images:

pairsmean angle θ (in u-space)mean chorddepth, along the ray / half-chorddepth, exact / half-chord
same image56∘27.223% (circle formula: 25%)10%
different images78∘35.134% (circle formula: 35%)12.5%

The ray-based depth matches the sphere formula tan(θ/4); the exact depth is smaller because the ellipsoid is elongated (the ratio of its longest to its shortest axis is 78), so it is nearer to the midpoint than the radial projection. Both are positive for every pair we tested, as the proposition says.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: with axis ratio 1 (a circle) the exact depth ratio equals tan(θ/4) shown in the last line; stretch the ellipse and the exact value drops below it. Move the two points close together: the depth tends to 0 but never reaches it, so the chord leaves the curve “as soon as it starts”. Tick the polygon: a polygon with vertices on the curve has only those vertices on it, and every edge dips inside by tan(π/2n) of its half-edge on a circle (0.58 for a triangle, 0.20 for 8 vertices). Because a polygon with at least three vertices cannot lie on the curve, the summands of a Minkowski sum on this curve must be single points.

What it excludes, and what it does not#

  • Excluded. The set-level claim: X=⨁Pi​ (or the union of such sums) cannot hold exactly for normalised tokens, whatever the archetypes. At best the hypothesis is a local approximation, valid at scales where the ellipsoid is flat.
  • Excluded as evidence. Signature 1 is automatic: a chord between two tokens leaves the set of attainable activations as soon as it starts (next section).
  • Not excluded. The per-activation statement. A token can still be a block-convex combination of archetypes: definition (ii) is a statement about each activation and survives, as does the linear one. Only the claim about the set fails. The linear hypothesis is affected in the same way (on E a code cannot be doubled), but its definition is also about each activation.
  • Not excluded. Earlier layers (before the last normalisation, where residual sums are exactly affine) and local statements at small scale.
Pitfall

The proposition does not say that the hypothesis is false. It says that a particular exact reading of it (a set that is a sum) is impossible after LayerNorm. Do not state it more strongly. Also check which layer is analysed: the proof concerns post-norm tokens; we assumed that the paper analyses them, as its footnote on ellipsoidal geometry suggests.

5. The three signatures under null models#

For each of the paper's three empirical signatures we ask what a model without archetypes gives. Chords leave the sample of a Gaussian too; archetypal analysis sits inside its sandwich where a Gaussian puts it; block co-activation follows image classes, the mark of a union, not of a sum.

The method is the same three times: (1) say what the paper shows; (2) build data whose geometry we control (a toy) and see what the diagnostic gives; (3) run the diagnostic on DINOv2 tokens and on a null model (a distribution with no archetype but the same first two moments) and on a twin network with random weights. The DINOv2 data are the patch tokens of 1,000 Imagenette images (ten classes), after the final normalisation; the toy scripts are in code/toy, the DINOv2 ones in code/dino (section 8). Table 1 summarises the outcome.

Table 1. The three signatures on DINOv2 tokens, on a null model without archetypes, and on planted structure. ρ: midpoint distance over chord (straight path / graph path). g: gap ratio at K=10.
DINOv2Null (no archetypes)Planted structure
(1) chords, ρ0.50 / 0.160.50 / 0.19 (Gaussian, same mean and covariance)0.49 / 0.15 (uniform in a simplex, d=50)
(2) AA, g0.470.51 (Gaussian per image)0.26 (ten-vertex polytope, same PCA error)
(3) blocksclasses (AMI 0.62)—union: 99.9% in blocks; sum: none (synthetic, R20)

Signature 1 — chords leave the sample, not the support#

In the paper §7.2 · p. 20, Fig. 17 left · p. 21

Take two tokens. Walk along the straight segment between them and, at each step, measure the distance to the nearest token of the data set; do the same along a shortest path in the k-nearest-neighbour graph. The straight path gives a triangle peaking at the midpoint (about 13), the graph path a plateau at 4–5. The authors read this as support for criterion (i), “compatible evidence, not proof”. Page 5 reads the panel: chords.

Idea

In high dimension a finite sample does not fill any body. The midpoint of two samples is farther from every sample than the two endpoints are, even when the midpoint belongs to a convex support. The graph path is within half an edge of a sample by construction, so it cannot leave the data. The triangle then says “the sample is finite and the dimension is large”, not “the support is non-convex”.

A heuristic with numbers. Draw samples from N(0,Id​). Two samples are at distance about 2d​, so the endpoint is at d/2​ from the midpoint. A third independent sample is at distance about d+d/2​=1.5d​ from the midpoint, which is 0.87 times the chord whatever d. For this third sample to beat an endpoint it must be at less than 0.5 times the chord; the nearest of N samples is closer than a typical one by a factor of about N−1/d. At d=50 and N=20,000 that factor is 0.82, giving 0.87×0.82≈0.7>0.5: an endpoint stays the nearest sample. At d=2 the factor is 0.007 and the midpoint is close to some sample. (An order-of-magnitude argument: the measured ρ is 0.01 at d=2 and 0.49 at d=50.)

Toy experiment t1_chords. N=20,000 points drawn uniformly in a regular simplex (one polytope), in a cube (a Minkowski sum of d segments), from a Gaussian, and on a sphere (the only non-convex support). ρ is the distance from the midpoint of a chord to the nearest sample divided by the chord; ρ=21​ means the nearest sample is an endpoint (the “triangle” of the paper). Mean over 200 random pairs.

simplex0.0110.0330.1060.2310.3700.4880.500

Gaussian0.0110.0390.1160.2530.3920.4960.500
sphere0.2340.2220.2390.3330.4600.5000.500

For the three convex supports, in which every chord stays inside the support, ρ grows from 0.01 at d=2 to 0.23–0.27 at d=10 and 0.49–0.50 from d=50. Only in low dimension does the sphere stand out. Filling does not help quickly: at d=20, ρ falls only from 0.44 to 0.34 (simplex) when N goes from 103 to 105; the log–log slope of the nearest-neighbour distance against N is −0.067, close to the −1/d=−0.05 of a filled d-dimensional body.

DINOv2 (r2_interpolation_nulls). We reproduce the paper's test on 50,000 post-norm tokens, 300 pairs, k=15 cosine neighbours, 101 steps, and run the same on null models:

How to read this figure
  • Panel (a). A schematic: the ellipsoid E, two tokens y,y′ on it, their chord and its midpoint m with the arrow “depth” down to the surface. The caption gives the measured values: tokens of one image are 56∘ apart, the depth is 10% of the half-chord (12.5% and 78∘ for different images). It is the picture of section 4.
  • Panel (b). x: dimension d of the toy space (N=20,000 points; the ticks 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 are equally spaced). y: ρ, the distance from the midpoint of a chord to the nearest sample over the chord length; 0.5 is the ceiling (the nearest sample is an endpoint). One curve per support. Look at where the curves meet the dashed line at 0.5: about d=50 for every convex support; the orange curve (sphere) starts high, near 0.23.
  • Panel (c). The paper's test: x position along the path, y distance to the nearest sample (normalised by the chord). Solid: straight path, a triangle with peak 0.5 at the middle, the same for DINOv2 (blue) and the Gaussian (grey). Dashed: graph path; DINOv2's is flat near 0.16, the Gaussian's has two bumps up to 0.37 near the ends (it has fewer, longer hops: 3.9 against 6.9).
  • Conclusion. The triangle is a property of finite samples in high dimension. A distribution with a convex support and no archetype gives the same figure as the tokens.
  • What it does not show. That the tokens are not a Minkowski sum: only that this test cannot say so. The null matches the first two moments only. The random twin is less extreme (0.43), so some of the tokens' behaviour does depend on training.
Our reading — caveat: the ellipsoid is a separate reason

For normalised tokens the chord leaves the support as well, for a reason unrelated to polytopes: the support is on an ellipsoid (section 4, Proposition). So the signature is automatic in two independent ways. The sphere row of the table shows that a curved support gives a large ρ even in low dimension, but a convex one gives it at d≥50 anyway, so the figure cannot tell the two cases apart.

Signature 2 — archetypal analysis in its sandwich#

In the paper §7.2 · p. 20, Fig. 17 middle · p. 21

Archetypal analysis (AA) fitted on the 256 tokens of one image reconstructs them with a mean squared error that falls with the number of archetypes: 0.32 (K=3), 0.26 (5), 0.19 (10), 0.138 (20), 0.116 (30), against 0.227 for the SAE (dashed). AA is the single-tile case of the hypothesis, so this is read as a direct test of convex coding. Reading of the panel: page 5.

Reminder — archetypal analysis and its sandwich

AA with K archetypes writes each data point as a convex combination of K archetypes, themselves convex combinations of data points. It has two natural neighbours: PCA and k-means. More.

Lemma — sandwich own

For any data set and any K, the optimal reconstruction errors satisfy err[PCAK−1​]≤err[AAK​]≤err[k-meansK​].

Proof, step by step
  1. Left inequality. The reconstructions of AAK​ are convex combinations of K points, so they lie in the affine hull of these K points, of dimension at most K−1.K points span an affine space of dimension at most K−1
  2. PCAK−1​ is the best reconstruction in an affine subspace of dimension K−1 (the mean plus K−1 principal directions).Eckart–Young for centred data
  3. Hence err[PCAK−1​]≤err[AAK​].AA's reconstructions are one candidate for PCA's minimisation
  4. Right inequality. A k-means solution has K centroids, each the average of the data points of its cluster. An average of data points is a convex combination of data points, so each centroid is an admissible archetype.archetypes must lie in the convex hull of the data
  5. The k-means reconstruction of a point is its centroid, which is the archetype with the one-hot code (0,…,1,…,0), a point of the simplex.codes of AA are in the simplex
  6. So every k-means solution is feasible for AA with the same error; the optimum of AA is at most that.minimum over a larger set
Worked example — a tiny data set

Five points in the plane, K=2: (0,0),(2,0),(4,0),(1,1.5),(3,1.5), errors as sums of squares. PCA with one component (a line through the mean (2,0.6)): error 2.70. Best k-means with two centroids: clusters {(0,0),(2,0),(1,1.5)} and {(4,0),(3,1.5)}, centroids (1,0.5) and (3.5,0.75), error 3.5+1.625=5.125. AA with two archetypes reconstructs on a segment between two points of the hull; a numerical optimisation (hill climbing, 60 restarts) gives an error of about 2.97, with archetypes near (0.34,0.51) and (3.66,0.51). Order: 2.70≤2.97≤5.125; the gap ratio is g=(2.97−2.70)/(5.125−2.70)=0.11. The k-means centroids are feasible archetypes, which is why AA cannot do worse than 5.125.

What the sandwich implies for the paper's figure. Per-image AA is a model refitted on each image, with K free archetypes for 256 tokens. The SAE is a single dictionary shared by all images, with 8 active atoms per token. We reproduce the paper's AA errors (0.32, 0.25, 0.18 against 0.32, 0.26, 0.19 for K=3,5,10), which lets us place the SAE's 0.227 on our axes. A k-means with ten centroids per image already passes below it (0.21), and so does PCA with nine components (0.15). “Matching the SAE with ten archetypes” is therefore not specific to convex mixing: it rewards any model refitted on each image.

The informative number is where AA sits inside its sandwich: g=(AA−PCA)/(k-means−PCA), between 0 (as good as PCA) and 1 (as bad as k-means), calibrated on data of known geometry.

Toy experiment t2_sandwich. 256 points in R50 with identical sample mean and covariance: mixtures of ten random Gaussian vertices with Dirichlet(0.5) weights plus noise (PCA(9) error ≈0.05), against a Gaussian with exactly the same mean and covariance. At K=10: g=0.19 for the polytope, g=0.49 for the Gaussian (20 repetitions); the polytope is below the Gaussian in all repetitions for K≥5. No sandwich violation in any run.

DINOv2 (r3_aa_sandwich). Per image, K=10, mean over 200 images (100 for the nulls):

datag at K=10
DINOv2 tokens, post-norm0.47 (s.e. 0.003)
Gaussian with the covariance of the same image0.51
ten-vertex polytope planted in the same image (same PCA(9) error)0.26
DINOv2 tokens, pre-norm0.40
random-weights twin, post-norm0.49
How to read this figure
  • Panel (a). x: number K of archetypes. y: mean squared error per coordinate. Three curves: PCA with K−1 components (lowest), AA (middle), k-means (highest). Crosses: the paper's AA values, which our AA curve passes through. Dashed horizontal line: the SAE, 0.227.
  • Look at. Where each curve crosses the dashed line (the y axis is logarithmic): k-means (0.21) and AA (0.18) are below it at K=10, and PCA, which is the lowest curve, is already near it at K=5 and at 0.15 with nine components. All three, not only AA, go below the SAE.
  • Panel (b). y: g between 0 (AA as good as PCA) and 1 (k-means level). Three data sets. A planted polytope sits low (0.26 at K=10), a Gaussian near 0.5, the tokens at 0.47. At very small K (2–3) the tokens lie above the Gaussian, so the ordering is not uniform in K; the paper's regime is K≥10.
  • Conclusion. AA's position inside its sandwich is barely closer to a small polytope than a Gaussian cloud is.
  • What it does not show. It does not exclude polytopes with many more than ten vertices, which behave like a smooth body, nor sums of several tiles; it is calibrated for ten vertices (the number the paper uses).
Our reading — the honest caveat

The test excludes “the token cloud of an image is a polytope with about ten vertices”, not “convex coding” in general. The tokens are somewhat closer to the polytope end than the Gaussian is (0.47 against 0.51), and the pre-norm tokens more so (0.40); the difference is small next to the planted polytope (0.26). We make no claim beyond that.

Signature 3 — a sum is not a union#

In the paper §7.2 · p. 20, Fig. 17 right · p. 21

The matrix Z⊤Z of the codes of an archetypal analysis with about 1,000 archetypes, reordered by clustering, is block-diagonal. This is offered as support for block structure. Reading of the panel: page 5.

Idea

Block-diagonal means: a token uses archetypes of one group only. That is a union of polytopes (clusters). A Minkowski sum of tiles that are active together predicts the opposite: an AA, whose codes live in a single simplex, has to take the sums of vertices as archetypes, and every token uses all of them at once.

Why a sum gives product weights
  1. Let x=p+q with p=∑i​αi​ai​∈P1​ and q=∑j​βj​bj​∈P2​, ∑i​αi​=∑j​βj​=1.two tiles active together
  2. x=∑i​αi​ai​⋅(∑j​βj​)+(∑i​αi​)⋅∑j​βj​bj​=∑i,j​αi​βj​(ai​+bj​).multiply p by ∑j​βj​=1 and q by ∑i​αi​=1
  3. The weights αi​βj​ are non-negative and sum to 1: a point of the simplex over the archetypes ai​+bj​.∑i,j​αi​βj​=(∑i​αi​)(∑j​βj​)=1
  4. Therefore the single-simplex AA of a sum has the vertex sums as archetypes, and the code of x is α⊗β.Kronecker product of the two codes
  5. The co-activation of this token is (α⊗β)(α⊗β)⊤=(αα⊤)⊗(ββ⊤), which has no zero entry as soon as all αi​,βj​>0.product of positive numbers
Worked example

Two tiles, each a segment: P1​=[a1​,a2​], P2​=[b1​,b2​], with α=(0.7,0.3) and β=(0.6,0.4). Sum. The four archetypes are a1​+b1​,a1​+b2​,a2​+b1​,a2​+b2​ and the code is (0.42,0.28,0.18,0.12), which sums to 1. The co-activation matrix of this token is

​0.1760.1180.0760.050​0.1180.0780.0500.034​0.0760.0500.0320.022​0.0500.0340.0220.014​​,
with no zero entry: every archetype co-activates with every other. Union. If the four archetypes are a1​,a2​,b1​,b2​ and a token uses one tile, the code is (0.7,0.3,0,0) and the matrix has a non-zero block (0.490.21​0.210.09​) and zeros elsewhere: blocks.

Toy experiment t3_sum_union. In R20, N=4000 points, Dirichlet(1) weights. U: a union of four separated triangles (K=12 archetypes). S: the Minkowski sum T1​+T2​ of two triangles (K=9 archetypes, the nine vertex sums). We cluster the normalised co-activation matrix and measure the share of off-diagonal co-activation inside the blocks.

share inside the blockssame for an unstructured matrixpairs of archetypes that co-activate
union of four triangles99.9% (four blocks)18%18%
sum of two triangles42% (best of the partitions tried: three blocks)36%97%

For the union, the four blocks hold 99.9% of the off-diagonal co-activation and the archetypes found are within 1.4% of the diameter of true vertices. For the sum, 97% of the pairs of archetypes co-activate and no partition into blocks does better than chance. The Kronecker structure predicted above is there: the co-activation of the generating product code differs from G1​⊗G2​ by only 1.9% (relative), and the AA's by 40%, because with K=9 it recovers the nine vertex sums only to within about 12% of the diameter.

DINOv2 (r5_coactivation). An AA with 200 archetypes on the tokens of 100 images (256 per image), co-activation Z⊤Z ordered by the class from which each archetype draws most of its usage.

95%of archetypes draw more than half of their usage from a single class (10% for a uniform spread)
52%of the off-diagonal co-activation links archetypes of the same dominant class (10% expected; permutation 95th percentile 11%)
0.62adjusted mutual information of a ten-block clustering with the classes (0.29 with the images)
How to read this figure
  • Axes and colours. Each panel is a square matrix indexed by archetypes (same order on both axes); the colour of entry (i,j) is the normalised co-activation Cij​/Cii​Cjj​​ of archetypes i and j (dark blue = 1, white = 0, square-root colour scale). The diagonal equals 1 by construction; in (c) black lines delimit the ten classes.
  • (a) Union. Four dark blocks of three archetypes on the diagonal, white elsewhere: each token lives in one triangle.
  • (b) Sum. Every entry is blue (moderately dark) with a faint product pattern: no block.
  • (c) DINOv2. Ten blocks along the diagonal, which are the ten classes. Off-diagonal mass is not zero: 57% of it is inside the ten blocks.
  • Conclusion. Tokens of similar objects share archetypes, which any clustering would show. The structure is that of a union of polytopes (the repaired definition of section 2), not of a sum of tiles.
  • What it does not show. That there is no additive structure at all: a single-simplex AA with 200 archetypes might not resolve a second tile (position, say) on top of the class. Also, 52% of the archetypes draw more than half of their usage from a single image: with 200 archetypes on 100 images, the archetypes partly describe images.
Our reading — honest caveat

Block structure is evidence for the union in the repaired definition, and against a reading where several tiles are active at once in this basis. It is not evidence for “additive tiles”, which is what the Minkowski sum needs. The global AA with 200 archetypes leaves 40% of the variance unexplained, against 46% for k-means with 200 clusters.

6. Identifiability: a gap, a repair, and a statement that is not specific#

The paper's proof that a Minkowski sum does not determine its summands has a gap, which a numerical counter-example shows. The true statement concerns supports with all tiles active, and it holds just as well for linear codes. What identifies a dictionary in practice is sparsity and the law of the codes.

In the paper Prop. 2 · p. 21, App. J Prop. 4 · p. 50

Consequence (I3): the decomposition of X into a Minkowski sum is not unique, so concepts cannot be recovered from the activations of one layer; one should use the attention weights and earlier layers. The proof passes to support functions, hA⊕B​=hA​+hB​ with hC​(u)=supx∈C​⟨u,x⟩, so that decomposing X means writing hX​ as a sum of sublinear functions. It then picks “any sublinear s with 0≤s≤hX​” and writes hX​=(hX​−s)+s. Full reading on page 5.

The gap#

s is a valid summand only if hX​−s is itself sublinear, i.e. the support function of a convex set. It is so exactly when the convex set with support function s is a summand of X. Being sublinear and below hX​ is not enough.

Counter-example with numbers own

Take for X the equilateral triangle of unit side centred at the origin, with vertices (±21​,−63​​) and (0,33​​), and the short segment Q=[−0.1,0.1]×{0}, which lies inside the triangle (its inradius is 0.289). Let s=hQ​, i.e. s(w)=0.1∣w1​∣. Then 0≤s≤hX​ (because Q⊂X). Now take the directions u=(cos60∘,sin60∘)=(0.5,0.866) and v=(cos120∘,sin120∘)=(−0.5,0.866) and f=hX​−s:

  • hX​(u)=0.5 (attained at a vertex), s(u)=0.05, so f(u)=0.45; the same for v: f(v)=0.45.
  • u+v=(0,3​): hX​(u+v)=33​​3​=1, s(u+v)=0, so f(u+v)=1.0.

Subadditivity would require f(u+v)≤f(u)+f(v)=0.9. But 1.0>0.9: f is not sublinear, so hX​−s is not a support function, and s is not a summand. In general with Q=[−ε,ε]×{0} the violation is exactly ε (0.1 here, 0.2 for ε=0.2). A grid of 3,600 directions finds a maximal violation of 0.173 (at 150∘ and 30∘) and 6.6% of the direction pairs violate it (t4_hexagon, part c).

A triangle has no summand other than its own homothets (and points), so no short segment is a summand of it: this is the reason (see page 5 for the proof).

The statement that is true#

Decompositions are never unique, for three trivial reasons: summands can be translated in opposite directions (P⊕Q=(P+t)⊕(Q−t)); a summand can be split, P=λP⊕(1−λ)P for a convex P (the segment [0,2]=[0,1]⊕[0,1]); summands can be regrouped. The rectangle that the paper cuts into three segments is an instance of the second and third. Up to these operations, a polytope is a sum of indecomposable ones, and that decomposition is not unique either: the hexagon (section 2) is the classical example, H=S1​⊕S2​⊕S3​=T⊕(−T), segments and triangles being indecomposable.

Remark — what we changed

We keep the paper's conclusion (decompositions of a support are not unique) but replace its proof: the paper's “any sublinear s” becomes “any s such that hX​−s is sublinear”, and the example is the hexagon, not a rectangle cut in segments.

The same holds for linear codes#

The corrected statement concerns the support of the activations when all tiles are active. Under the same reading the linear hypothesis fares no better: the set {∑j​zj​dj​: z∈[0,M]c} generated by a dense linear code is a zonotope, and the hexagon shows that it does not determine its generators, nor even whether it comes from a linear code. Nobody concludes from this that sparse dictionaries cannot be learned from one layer.

What makes dictionaries identifiable in practice#

  • Sparsity. If each input uses at most k atoms, the data lie on a union of low-dimensional subspaces, and under conditions on the dictionary (small coherence, see coherence) the dictionary is unique up to sign and permutation. This is a property of the law on the support, not of the support.
  • Independence and non-Gaussianity. Independent non-Gaussian coordinates identify the mixing matrix up to scale and permutation (independent component analysis).

The hypothesis has the same resources. Item (ii) is a sparsity assumption; it turns the support into the union of section 2, whose low-dimensional pieces expose the individual polytopes. And the two clouds of the hexagon figure, which share their support, are told apart at a glance.

Our reading — consequence (I3) is too strong as stated

“Concepts cannot be recovered from the activations of one layer” does not follow from non-uniqueness of the support's decomposition, any more than for sparse dictionaries. The practical advice of the paper stands on its own merits: attention weights are available, and they are the codes of the decomposition of Proposition 1.

7. A tile that can be observed: position#

One factor of variation has a known value for every token: its position on the 16×16 grid. Its code in the last layer is a sum of a row effect and a column effect to 97.4%: two one-dimensional factors, a curved box, not a simplex.

In the paper §6 · p. 15–16, Fig. 14–15 · p. 16, §5 · p. 11, Fig. 9

The position of a token can be decoded linearly in the early layers and less in the last ones; the stable rank of the position basis falls from about 9 to about 2.7 and the two leading principal components explain about all of its variance in the last layers: a two-dimensional sheet. In the dictionary, three dense atoms (“left”, “right”, “bottom”) fire on roughly a quarter of all tokens each, and some atoms form antipodal pairs. See page 4.

The paper reads this as a first hint of dense, non-sparse structure. We ask which of the two geometries of section 2 the position code has.

The additive test#

Reminder — an additive two-way table

A table Pij​ with i indexing rows and j columns is additive if Pij​=ri​+cj​: the effect of the row and that of the column simply add. Here each entry is a vector of R768. The best additive fit of a table is given by the row means and column means (after subtracting the overall mean), and the share of variance it explains is R2=1−∥P−P^∥2/∥P∥2. A table that is a sum of a row effect and a column effect is a Minkowski sum of two sets: the set of row effects and the set of column effects, with no coupling between the two.

Worked example

The 2×3 table (13​24​46​) is additive: r=(0,2), c=(1,2,4), R2=1. Change one entry: (13​25​46​). The additive fit now leaves the residual (61​−61​​−31​31​​61​−61​​) and R2=0.981. For a 16×16 table with 255 degrees of freedom after centring, the additive model has 15+15=30: a table with no structure (random) would give R2=30/255=11.8%, the baseline against which 97.4% is judged.

Experiment (r6_position_additive). Let Pij​∈R768 be the mean token at position (i,j) over the 1,000 images, centred. Last layer, after the final normalisation.

97.4%of the variance of P explained by ri​+cj​ (44% rows, 53% columns)
94.7%held-out: fit on 500 images, scored on the table of the other 500; ceiling 95.2%
11.8%a generic table (30 of 255 degrees of freedom)

The held-out figure is the honest one: the tables of two halves of the images are noisy, so even the exact table of one half explains only 95.2% of the other's (the ceiling). The additive fit reaches 94.7%, within half a point of it. Each factor is close to one-dimensional:

one directiontwo directions
row effects ri​ (16 vectors)72%96%
column effects cj​ (16 vectors)77%97%

The coordinate along the leading direction is monotone in the index (rank correlation 1.0 for both), and the two leading directions are orthogonal (cosine 0.05). A straight line in the index would explain only 71% and 75%: the factors are arcs, not segments, as the curvature of the ellipsoid imposes. The two rank-one factors together explain 72.8% of P.

How to read this figure
  • Axes. x: first principal component of P (41% of its variance); y: second (32%); together 73%. Each blue dot is the mean token at one of the 256 positions.
  • Grey lattice. The additive fit ri​+cj​ plotted in the same plane: 16 curves for fixed i (varying j) and 16 for fixed j.
  • Look at. The dots form a curved sheet and sit on the lattice: each position is reached by combining a row arc and a column arc.
  • Conclusion. The sheet that the paper finds is a product: a sum of two one-dimensional factors.
  • What it does not show. The scatter around the lattice (about 3% of the variance outside the additive model); and that training created additivity: the in-sample R2 is also 0.91 before the last normalisation and 0.90 for the random-weights twin, so the test establishes the shape of the table, not its origin. Position is also only 4.8% of the variance of a token.

Why this is “a box”#

The 16×16 grid of positions is the product of a row range and a column range, and the code is the sum of the corresponding factors. The row and the column vary freely and independently: there is no unit budget shared between them. In the terms of section 2, this is a linear code with two bounded features (a zonotope, here curved), not a tile with a simplex of archetypes: a box, not a simplex. A simplex tile would predict that tokens sit near archetypes (corners); the position grid is uniform.

Our reading — it explains two anomalies of the paper's dictionary
  • Dense atoms. A non-negative, sparse code has to represent a signed axis (left-to-right) by two opposite atoms; and an axis on which every token has a value is always active. This explains atoms such as “left”, “right”, “bottom” that fire on about a quarter of all tokens each.
  • Antipodal pairs. Two atoms di​≈−dj​ are the two signs of one axis.

This is the axis code the paper itself describes; it does not need polytopes. Where the paper uses position as a first hint of non-linear structure, we read it as the linear special case.

Checked on DINOv2 — r6_position_additive, r7_position_layers

Additive R2: 0.974 (trained, post-norm), 0.909 (trained, pre-norm), 0.904 (random twin, post-norm). Held-out for the trained post-norm: 0.947 against a ceiling 0.952. r6 also gives the stable rank of the centred table (2.4) and the position share of token variance (4.8%); r7 follows position across the 13 depths. See section 8.

8. The lab: how the experiments are organised#

Every number of this page comes from one of eleven scripts in code/; each writes one results file with its versions, seeds and running time. The DINOv2 ones read a feature cache written once by r0_extract.py.

Data, model, conventions#

  • Model. DINOv2 ViT-B/14 with 4 registers (dinov2_vitb14_reg, LVD-142M weights), and a random-weights twin (same architecture, torch.manual_seed(0), no pre-training). CPU only.
  • Data. Imagenette (ten ImageNet classes), 320 px validation split. 1,000 “statistics” images (the first 100 file names of each class, sorted) and 200 held-out images (the next 20 per class). Preprocessing: shorter side 256 (bicubic), centre crop 224, ImageNet mean and standard deviation. Each image gives 256 patch tokens; the image lists are in r0_image_lists.json.
  • Toy data. Synthetic, generated inside each script; all seeds are fixed, so a rerun reproduces the files exactly.
  • Files. Every DINOv2 JSON file has a versions block (package versions, model identifier, weights SHA-256), a written date and runtime_s. Large features live outside the repository and are written by r0_extract.py.

Experiment → script → results → what it measures#

How to rerun#

From code/: python toy/t1_chords.py (and t2–t4), then once python dino/r0_extract.py (it needs the model weights and the Imagenette validation split, and writes the cache), then python dino/rN_*.py in any order. The shared code is in code/rh/ (aa.py archetypal analysis, interp.py chord test and neighbour graph, nulls.py null models, dino.py model loading) and code/dino/common.py; code/tests/test_core.py tests the core functions.

What would be needed to go further#

  • The paper's dictionary. We did not have the 32,000-atom SAE. The experiment that our analysis calls for, a test of box or simplex on its codes, needs it: for groups of atoms, do the codes fill a square or a triangle (section 2)? Ideally on factors of known value, categorical (a simplex is plausible) against continuous (we found a box).
  • Before the last normalisation, or with convexity understood along the ellipsoid (section 4).
  • Per-head analysis. With the attention weights as codes, look for tiles head by head, keeping in mind that all heads are active and the polytopes move with the image.
  • Scale. We used one model, 1,000 images of ten classes and at most 50,000 tokens; null models match first and second moments only. These are checks, not benchmarks.

9. Errata: slips and inconsistencies in the paper#

Thirteen items, none of which changes the paper's main findings; they matter for a careful reading of Part III and of the figures. Stated factually, with the evidence.

References are to the arXiv v3 PDF and its figures. The first ten items were checked against the source and the figures; items 11–14 are from our reading of the appendices and are worth re-checking against the cited place before being quoted.

10. Summary and reflexes#

What to remember
  1. Verdict. Parts I and II are measurements and stand. In Part III the attention lemma is a theorem; the arguments for the hypothesis do not separate it from simpler pictures; one exact consequence fails after the last normalisation.
  2. Nested. The definition is repaired to a union over active sets, X=⋃S​⨁i∈S​Pi​. A bounded linear code is the case of segment tiles ({0,Mdj​}, or {−Mdj​,Mdj​} for signs). What separates the hypotheses is a box or a simplex inside a tile; the hexagon is one support for both.
  3. Attention. The statement holds for random weights; the polytopes are rebuilt per image; rank 64≪261; attention spread over 33–78 tokens with 10–49% on the five special tokens; tokens are 0.65 attention / 0.35 MLP, but 0.46 / 0.54 within an image; the last block carries 82%.
  4. LayerNorm. Outputs lie on an ellipsoid (∥u∥2=d to 10−7, 0.19≤γ≤14.9) which contains no segment: no non-trivial Minkowski sum fits. A chord's midpoint is (1−cos2θ​)d​ below the sphere; measured exactly, 10% (same image) and 12.5% (different images) of the half-chord. The per-activation statements survive.
  5. Signatures. (1) ρ=0.50 and 0.16 on tokens, 0.50 and 0.19 on a Gaussian: chords leave a sample, not a support. (2) PCAK−1​≤AAK​≤k-meansK​; g=0.47 on tokens, 0.51 Gaussian, 0.26 planted polytope; large polytopes are not excluded. (3) A sum gives product weights αi​βj​ and a dense matrix; a union gives blocks; DINOv2 has blocks that are the classes (AMI 0.62).
  6. Identifiability. The proof needs hX​−s sublinear (counter-example 0.45, 0.45, 1.0); the true statement is about supports, holds for zonotopes, and sparsity and the law of the codes are what identify dictionaries.
  7. Position. Pij​≈ri​+cj​: 97.4% (held-out 94.7% against a ceiling of 95.2%; 11.8% for a generic table), factors one-dimensional (72% / 77%, 96% / 97% with two directions): a box, which explains the dense and the antipodal atoms.

Reflexes#

  • When you see “sum of tiles, few active” → union over active sets; a full sum is convex.
  • When you see “a bounded feature” → a segment tile; the hypotheses differ only by box against simplex inside a group.
  • When you see “softmax output is a convex combination” → true for any weights; ask what is fixed across images, whether the polytope can be filled (rank), and what else is added to the token (MLPs, LayerNorm).
  • When you see “LayerNorm” → centre, scale: points on a sphere in 1⊥, then an invertible affine map: an ellipsoid; no segments.
  • When you see “the midpoint of two samples is far from the data” → try a Gaussian with the same moments.
  • When you see “AA with K archetypes” → place it between PCA(K−1) and k-means(K); report g.
  • When you see “block-diagonal co-activation” → union of clusters; a sum gives a dense Kronecker pattern.
  • When you see “decomposition is not unique” → true of supports, for zonotopes too; ask what the law of the codes says.
  • When you see “a dense, signed or antipodal feature” → try an additive (box) code first.

What the next page does with it#

Page 7 turns the whole guide into questions with answers, the ten-minute talk and a glossary.

11. Exercises#

Exercise 1 — Nested hypotheses with signed codes ★

Let x=∑j∈S​zj​dj​ with ∣zj​∣≤M. (a) Prove that x is block-convex with tiles Tj​={−Mdj​,Mdj​}. (b) Take M=2, z1​=−0.5, d1​=(1,0): give the code of the tile. (c) Why is the tile {0,Mdj​} not enough for signed codes?

Hint

Look for λ∈[0,1] with (1−λ)(−Md)+λMd=zd.

Solution

(a) Put λj​=(zj​+M)/(2M), in [0,1] because −M≤zj​≤M. Then (1−λj​)(−Mdj​)+λj​Mdj​=(2λj​−1)Mdj​=zj​dj​, a point of the tile with code (1−λj​,λj​) in Δ2. Summing over S gives block-convex coding with the same active set.

(b) λ1​=(−0.5+2)/4=0.375, code (0.625,0.375): 0.625(−2,0)+0.375(2,0)=(−0.5,0).

(c) The segment from 0 to Mdj​ only contains non-negative multiples of dj​; a negative zj​ is outside it.

Exercise 2 — Depth of a chord ★

Tokens after layer normalisation in d=768 have ∥u∥=d​. Two tokens subtend θ=90∘ in u-space. (a) Compute the depth of the midpoint of their chord below the sphere, the half-chord, and their ratio. (b) Same for θ=56∘ (the mean of tokens of one image). (c) Why is the measured exact depth on the real ellipsoid smaller than (b)'s ratio?

Hint

The midpoint has norm d​cos(θ/2); the half-chord is d​sin(θ/2).

Solution

(a) 768​=27.71. Depth =(1−cos45∘)⋅27.71=8.12; half-chord =27.71sin45∘=19.60; ratio tan22.5∘=0.414.

(b) Depth =(1−cos28∘)⋅27.71=3.24; half-chord =27.71sin28∘=13.01; ratio tan14∘=0.249. (The measured ray-based ratio on DINOv2 is 0.231, matching.)

(c) The real set is an ellipsoid with axis ratio 78; the nearest point of an elongated surface to the midpoint is nearer than the radial projection, so the exact depth is 10% of the half-chord, not 23–25%.

Exercise 3 — The sandwich on a tiny data set ★★

Data: (0,0),(2,0),(4,0),(1,1.5),(3,1.5), K=2 (errors are sums of squares). (a) Compute the error of PCA with one component and of the best k-means with two centroids. (b) Show that the pair of archetypes (0.5,0.5), (3.5,0.5) is feasible for archetypal analysis and compute its error. (c) Check the order of the lemma.

Hint

PCA: the mean is (2,0.6); the first singular direction is the x axis up to a small tilt (use a numerical SVD or compare with the value in the solution). Archetypes must lie in the convex hull of the data; reconstruct each point by its projection on the segment between the archetypes.

Solution

(a) PCA1​: 2.70 (from the singular values of the centred matrix). k-means: clusters {(0,0),(2,0),(1,1.5)} and {(4,0),(3,1.5)}, centroids (1,0.5) and (3.5,0.75), error 3.5+1.625=5.125.

(b) The hull has the left edge x=32​y and the right edge x=4−32​y; at height 0.5 it spans x∈[0.33,3.67], so (0.5,0.5) and (3.5,0.5) are inside. Projections on the segment y=0.5, x∈[0.5,3.5]: (0,0)→(0.5,0.5), error 0.5; (2,0)→(2,0.5), 0.25; (4,0)→(3.5,0.5), 0.5; (1,1.5) and (3,1.5) project straight down: 1 each. Total 3.25.

(c) 2.70≤3.25≤5.125. Better archetypes (a numerical search finds about 2.97) still satisfy 2.70≤2.97.

Exercise 4 — A sum gives a dense matrix, a union gives blocks ★★

Two tiles are segments [a1​,a2​] and [b1​,b2​]. A token has codes α=(0.5,0.5) and β=(0.25,0.75). (a) Give its code over the vertex sums ai​+bj​ and show that its co-activation matrix has no zero. (b) A union token uses only the first tile with code (0.5,0.5) over (a1​,a2​,b1​,b2​): give its matrix. (c) Show that for the sum the matrix is a Kronecker product.

Hint

The code over the sums is α⊗β; the co-activation of one token is its code times its transpose.

Solution

(a) α⊗β=(0.125,0.375,0.125,0.375), which sums to 1. Its outer product has entries wa​wb​>0 for every pair: no zero (the smallest is 0.0156).

(b) The code is (0.5,0.5,0,0) and the matrix is (0.250.25​0.250.25​) in the top-left block, zero elsewhere.

(c) (α⊗β)(α⊗β)⊤=(αα⊤)⊗(ββ⊤) by the mixed-product property of the Kronecker product.

Exercise 5 — Another segment violates subadditivity ★★

X is the unit equilateral triangle of the text, Q={0}×[−ε,ε] (vertical), s=hQ​, f=hX​−s. Take u=(cos30∘,sin30∘) and v=(0,−1). Compute f(u), f(v), f(u+v) and the violation of subadditivity. Does it depend on ε?

Hint

s(w)=ε∣w2​∣. The vertices are (±21​,−0.2887) and (0,0.5774).

Solution

hX​(u)=0.2887 (vertices (0.5,−0.2887) and (0,0.5774) both give 0.2887), hX​(v)=0.2887, u+v=(0.866,−0.5) and hX​(u+v)=0.5774 at the vertex (0.5,−0.2887). With s(u)=0.5ε, s(v)=ε, s(u+v)=0.5ε: f(u)=0.2887−0.5ε, f(v)=0.2887−ε, f(u+v)=0.5774−0.5ε. So f(u+v)−f(u)−f(v)=ε>0 for every ε>0 (for ε=0.1: 0.527 against 0.428). Subadditivity fails, so s is not a summand. The violation equals ε, as for the horizontal segment.

Exercise 6 — Stable rank against explained variance, and the null of the additive fit ★★★

(a) Show that a centred matrix whose top-2 principal components explain a share R2 of the variance has stable rank at most 2/R2; apply it to R2=0.99 and to the reported stable rank 2.6–2.8 of Fig. 14. (b) A 16×16 table has 255 degrees of freedom after centring and the additive model has 30: what R2 does an unstructured table get on average, and why? (c) Explain why the held-out R2 of the additive fit of the position table is compared with a ceiling.

Hint

(a) σ1​≥σ2​. (b) The additive fit is the orthogonal projection on a subspace of dimension 30 of a space of dimension 255; for an isotropic random table the projected share of squared norm is the ratio of dimensions.

Solution

(a) σ12​+σ22​=R2∥P∥F2​ and σ12​≥21​(σ12​+σ22​), so stable rank =∥P∥F2​/σ12​≤2/R2. For R2=0.99: 2.02. A value of 2.6–2.8 contradicts it, so the two panels cannot describe the same centred matrix.

(b) 30/255=11.8%: for a table with isotropic random entries, the projection onto a fixed 30-dimensional subspace keeps on average 30/255 of the squared norm. So 97.4% is far above chance.

(c) The table of each half of the images is a noisy estimate of the true table. Even the exact table of one half explains only part of the other's variance (95.2%): this is the best any model can do. The additive fit reaches 94.7%, so it is within 0.5 point of the maximum.
